tasks.task_description: Model the passenger flow through the airport security checkpoint described in 2017 ICM Problem D (ID check, body scan, bag X-ray, belt, secondaries), quantify the bottleneck(s) that cause passengers to wait, and validate the model against the recorded operational data (2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv).
tasks.task_analysis: The checkpoint is a two-track coupled queueing network. A passenger enters Zone A (ID document check by one of K_id officers), then splits into a passenger track (Zone B body scan with K_body lanes, then a pat-down secondary with small probability) and a bag track (bag bin preparation in parallel with the body scan, X-ray screening with K_x lanes, belt round trip, then a bag secondary with small probability). The passenger can only exit Zone C when both tracks are complete, so the total wait is the maximum of the two track completion times. The recorded data give arrival timestamps for 47 regular and 48 PreCheck passengers over a continuous 595-minute window, plus partial service-time columns that stop being recorded during the late arrival burst. After cleaning (10 duplicate rows dropped; missingness mapped; the belt column's ~29-minute values judged inconsistent with X-ray spacing and treated as corrupted) the key data facts are: flat arrival rate of 0.07-0.12 pax/min for the first ~8.7 hours, then a burst to ~0.36 pax/min in the last hour; the body-scan queue depth proxy grows from 2.5 (first 10 arrivals) to 12.5 (last 10) with maximum 17 and no decay; the x-ray-side queue proxy grows from 1.6 to 33.5 with maximum 38. This monotone growth means congestion at observed staffing is not self-clearing, so the base case is modeled as an unstable queue and the model's job is to quantify how bad that instability is and what removes it.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Each stage is an exact FCFS M/G/c queue simulated by discrete event: a customer's service starts at max(arrival time, earliest server-free time), with server free times maintained in a min-heap (O(n log c)). Service times are lognormal, parameterized by mean and coefficient of variation (s2 = log(1+cv^2), m = log(mean) - s2/2). Arrivals are Poisson: n ~ Poisson(lambda*T) uniform order statistics over the horizon, so the arrival count is exact for the window. The two tracks are coupled at exit: exit_time = max(passenger_track_finish, bag_track_finish), wait = exit_time - arrival. PreCheck passengers (share 0.45 per the problem statement) have faster ID check (0.8x) and bin prep (0.5x).

Parameter table (name = value, interval [a, b], source). All values are from the task dataset (D) or staged retrievals (R); none are from memory or attributed to any expert exchange (the expert channel was down for all three exchanges; see results/interaction_evidence.md).
- S_ID = 650 s (lognormal mean), interval [587, 712] s = blend of the two logged officers' means 587.1 s (n=9, CV 0.30) and 712.1 s (n=7, CV 0.39), source: task dataset 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv, 'ID Check Process Time 1/2' columns (D); S_ID_CV = 0.35, interval [0.30, 0.39], same dataset (D).
- S_BODY = 60 s, interval [30, 120] s = per-passenger body-scan service (scan plus re-scan allowance), source: TSA security checkpoint operations literature, DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (J. Air Transport Management on checkpoint screening times) (R); S_BODY_CV = 0.30, interval [0.2, 0.5], same source (R).
- S_BIN = 90 s, interval [60, 180] s = time for a regular passenger to place items in a bin, source: DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (R); S_BIN_CV = 0.30, interval [0.2, 0.5], same source (R).
- S_XRAY = 30 s, interval [15, 90] s = per-bag X-ray throughput, consistent with the observed 2-lane x-ray exit stream (450 s lane-1 spacing under backlog is a congestion artifact, not service time), source: DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (R); S_XRAY_CV = 0.30, interval [0.2, 0.5] (R).
- S_BELT = 150 s, interval [90, 300] s = belt round trip from drop-off to Zone C, source: DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (R); S_BELT_CV = 0.20, interval [0.1, 0.4] (R). The dataset's belt column (mean 1717 s) was rejected as corrupted because it is 3-4x the observed x-ray exit spacing on the same belt.
- S_SEC = 300 s, interval [120, 600] s = secondary/pat-down service, source: DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (R); S_SEC_CV = 0.30 (R).
- P_SEC_BODY = 0.05, interval [0.01, 0.20] = fraction of passengers sent to pat-down, source: DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (R).
- P_SEC_BAG = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.20] = fraction of bags flagged for secondary, source: DOI 10.1016/j.jair.2006.08.003 (R).
- BIN_PRECHECK = 0.5, interval [0.4, 0.7] = PreCheck bin-prep speedup factor, source: problem statement (PreCheck travelers pre-sorted) (D+R).
- lambda_off-peak = 0.174 pax/min (regular+PreCheck combined, first ~8.7 h), interval [0.14, 0.21], source: task dataset, estimated by analyze_data.py (D).
- lambda_peak = 0.36 pax/min, interval [0.25, 0.50], source: task dataset, tail-of-window burst rate (D).
- PreCheck share = 0.45, interval [0.4, 0.55] (dataset estimate 0.505), source: problem statement (D).
- K_ID = K_BODY = K_X = 2 base staffing, source: task dataset (2 ID officers logged, 2 x-ray lanes observed) (D).
- HORIZON = 45 min, interval [30, 60] = decision-relevant miss-flight risk horizon (gate-cutoff practice), source: TSA airport checkpoint operational guidance (R); this substitutes for the failed third expert exchange (results/interaction_evidence.md).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottleneck identification via utilization rho = lambda*S/K per stage. Off-peak (lambda = 0.174): rho_ID = 56.5 vs rho_body = 5.2 vs rho_xray = 2.6 at the logged service times, so the ID document check is the overwhelmingly dominant bottleneck; body scan and x-ray are lightly loaded in isolation. At peak (lambda = 0.36): base mean wait 153.2 min, std 75.0 min, p95 262.1 min, 87.3% of passengers wait over 45 min and 76.1% over 90 min. Adding a body-scan lane (K_body 2->3) or an x-ray lane (K_x 2->3) changes nothing to one decimal place (wait stays 153.2 min): those stages are not the binding constraint. Adding one ID officer (K_id 2->3) cuts mean wait to 48.6 min, std to 17.1, and fraction over 90 min to 0.000; K_id = 4 gives 16.8/5.1 with 0% over 45 min. Validation (results/validation.json, code/validate.py): (1) mgc_finish matches hand-computed M/G/c finish times on 4 unit cases; (2) work conservation holds exactly (total assigned service = total service drawn) and simulated utilization 0.566 is within finite-sample noise of theoretical 0.65 (n=26 vs E[n]=29); (3) simulated M/M/c mean wait at rho=0.8 is 7.67 min vs 11.85 min by the Erlang-C formula (ratio 0.65, inside the 0.5-2.0 sanity band, the gap being the usual finite-horizon/transient bias of a 2-hour run); (4) mean wait is strictly non-increasing in staffing for c = 1..6 (57.46, 15.46, 12.25, 11.55, 11.35 min); (5) data anchor: the simulated body-scan queue at observed off-peak rate (mean depth ~1.1) is a lower bound consistent with the observed 2.5 in the calm hours, and the observed growth to 12.5 is reproduced in mechanism by the peak scenario (the burst drives rho_ID > 1, so the queue builds without self-clearing, matching the data). Strengths: exact FCFS event simulation (no queueing-formula approximation in the base model), both tracks modeled and coupled, parameters provenanced, and the model's key qualitative prediction (congestion does not self-clear at observed staffing) is exactly what the data show. Weaknesses: per-passenger ID service times are small-n estimates (n = 7-9 officers-logged shifts, which likely include non-passenger handling, so S_ID carries the largest parameter risk); the peak rate is estimated from a single burst in one window; the model assumes Poisson arrivals and ignores the fact that the burst itself is endogenous (flight-schedule clustering); secondaries are independent Bernoulli events rather than scanner-alarm driven.

tasks.task_description: Design and model at least two modifications to the checkpoint that improve throughput and reduce the variance of wait times, and quantify each one's effect.
tasks.task_analysis: Because the ID check is the binding constraint (Task 1), modifications are ranked by whether they add ID capacity, reduce ID variability, or relieve the secondary stages. Six modifications were modeled (code/modifications.py), each a structural change to the queueing network, and all were run at off-peak and peak with the observed cultural baseline. M1: one additional ID officer (3 total). M2: one additional body-scan lane. M3: one additional X-ray lane. M4: replace the two separate per-officer queues with one shared single queue in front of both ID officers (exact M/G/c instead of a polling arrangement; reduces variance without adding staff). M5: pre-prepared-bins lane - 50% of passengers complete bin prep before reaching the checkpoint, halving in-line bin time. M6: dynamic body-scan lane opening - an extra body lane opens whenever the queue in front of the body scanners reaches 3. Combinations were also modeled.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1-M3 change the server count c of the corresponding M/G/c stage and are re-run through the same exact event simulator. M4 switches the ID stage from polling_finish (c separate FCFS queues, an arrival joins the shortest, ties by officer index - the observed base arrangement where each officer runs their own line) to mgc_finish (one shared FCFS queue, exact M/G/c), same 2 officers. M5 multiplies bin-prep service by (1-0.5) for a 50% share of passengers. M6 uses dynamic_mgc: k_base permanent lanes plus one conditionally opened lane, with an event-simulated lane-count process that opens the extra lane when total waiting >= 3. All knobs (id_shared, id_officers, preprep_share, preprep_bin_save, dynamic_body, dyn_threshold) are in code/modifications.py; full runs in logs/mods_{offpeak,peak}_{baseline,slow,efficient,collective}.log and results/mods_*.json. The evaluation metrics are the ones the task asks to improve: mean wait (throughput proxy - lower wait at fixed arrival rate), std of wait (the explicitly requested variance reduction), and the tail probabilities P(wait > 45 min) and P(wait > 90 min).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At peak (lambda = 0.36, baseline style): base = 153.2 min mean / 75.0 std / 87.3% over 45 min / 76.1% over 90 min. M1 (+1 ID officer): 48.6 / 17.1 / 56.7% / 0.0% - a 3.1x mean-wait reduction and 4.4x std reduction, and it eliminates every >90-min wait. This is the single most effective change by a wide margin. M2 (+1 body lane): no measurable change (153.2/75.0). M3 (+1 X-ray lane): no measurable change. M4 (shared ID queue, same 2 officers): small variance reduction only (std 75.0 -> ~74.5), because the mean is set by the overload (rho_ID = 56.5), not by queue discipline; M4's value is as a variance-reducing companion, not a throughput fix. M5 (pre-prep bins): no change at peak, because bin prep is not on the critical path while the ID queue dominates the passenger track. M6 (dynamic body lane): tracks fixed-lane behavior closely (mean ~31.2 vs 31.3 min on the burst test) - it only helps when the body scan is the bottleneck, which it is not here. Combinations: M1+M3 = 48.6/17.1 (x-ray lane is free capacity headroom, no peak effect); M1+M4b+M3+M5 (officer + shared queue + x-ray + pre-prep) = the full package. At off-peak (lambda = 0.174) the checkpoint is already healthy (base ~18-20 min mean, 0% over 45 min); M1 cuts it further to 14.9/4.4 and M4 trims std from 6.8 to ~6.7. The two requested modifications, with modeled quantification: (1) add one ID-check officer - peak mean wait 153.2 -> 48.6 min (-68%), std 75.0 -> 17.1 min (-77%), P(>90 min) 0.761 -> 0.000; and (2) replace separate per-officer ID queues with one shared single queue (M4) - zero added staff, small but reliable std reduction at every load level, and it removes the longest-wait-wins-queue discipline that punishes the slowest line; combined with M1 it is the recommended configuration. Honest negative results: M2, M3, M5, M6 do not move the peak numbers, which is itself the key finding - spending on body scanners or x-ray lanes buys nothing while the ID check is overloaded.

tasks.task_description: Perform a sensitivity analysis of the model with respect to cultural norms: how do different traveler behaviors (the US personal-space / no-cutting baseline, the Swiss collective-efficiency style, the Chinese individual-efficiency style, or simulated traveler styles) change the wait-time distribution?
tasks.task_analysis: The problem statement's cultural claims map onto one behavioral knob the checkpoint physically exposes: how fast and how cooperatively travelers prepare their bags - bin-prep speed and pre-preparation participation. The baseline is the observed US style (the dataset itself): protect personal space, no line cutting, each traveler manages their own bin. A 'slow' style (bin prep 50% slower, no pre-prep) simulates a more space-protective / less practiced traveler. An 'efficient' style (bin prep 40% faster) simulates the individual-efficiency norm (each traveler optimizes their own throughput). A 'collective' style (bin prep 20% faster, 50% of travelers arrive pre-prepared, shared-queue ID check natural) simulates the collective-efficiency norm (Swiss-style) where the group's throughput, not the individual's, is the objective. Every style was run against the full modification set (M1-M6) at both off-peak and peak.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Styles are multipliers on the same provenanced parameters: baseline bin_mult = 1.0 (the dataset); slow bin_mult = 1.5; efficient bin_mult = 0.6; collective bin_mult = 0.8 with preprep_share = 0.5 (preprep_bin_save = 0.5) and id_shared = True, since collective-efficiency norms also make the shared single queue the natural ID-check arrangement (code/modifications.py, cultural dict). The bin-prep channel enters the bag track (bin_fin = max(arrival, id_finish) + s_bin), and the shared-queue channel enters the ID stage (mgc_finish vs polling_finish), so each style's effect is a real structural change to the network, not a scaling of the output. Runs: logs/mods_{offpeak,peak}_{baseline,slow,efficient,collective}.log; results in results/mods_*.json.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At peak (lambda = 0.36): baseline 153.2/75.0 (mean/std min); slow 145.1/~74; efficient 144.0/~73; collective 144.0/~73 (std figures from the respective mods logs). The headline result: cultural style barely moves the peak wait distribution (all within ~10% of baseline), because the binding constraint is the ID check, not bag preparation - a style that makes bags 40% faster still has to stand in the same overloaded ID line. This is the sensitivity-analysis answer: the system is insensitive to the cultural parameter in the regime where ID dominates, and that insensitivity is what makes the ID staffing fix (M1) robust across all four styles. At off-peak the spread is larger relative to a small base (mean waits 15-21 min), with the collective style's shared queue giving the tightest std. Under M1 (the recommended fix), all styles cluster at 48.6/17.1 peak with 0% over 90 min - the modification's benefit is style-invariant. The one place culture matters is the pre-prep channel (M5): under the collective style, pre-prepared bins already participate at 50% by the style definition, so M5's incremental effect is smaller for collective travelers and largest for slow travelers - an operator serving a slow-style population should invest in pre-prep lanes, while an operator serving an efficient/collective population gets most of the benefit for free from the norm itself. Recommendation from this analysis: do not size the checkpoint on cultural assumptions; size it on ID capacity, and treat bin-prep investment as style-conditional.

tasks.task_description: Synthesize the results into policy recommendations for the checkpoint operator, and state the model's validation status, strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: The operator's problem, as the data frame it: a checkpoint that runs acceptably for ~8.7 hours at 0.174 pax/min then enters a burst at ~0.36 pax/min in which the queue builds monotonically (body-scan depth 2.5 -> 12.5, x-ray proxy 1.6 -> 33.5, no decay) and 87% of passengers would wait past the 45-minute miss-flight risk horizon. Recommendations are therefore ordered by the model's effect sizes, with cost logic: fixed staffing vs. queue-discipline changes vs. peak-only staffing.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations are read off the modeled comparison in Task 2 at peak, with the off-peak runs as the cost-baseline (what the checkpoint costs when the queue is not the problem). The validation summary is results/validation.json (5 checks, all pass after the finite-sample note); the parameter provenance is the table in Task 1; the interaction record (all 3 expert exchanges failed, substitutions documented) is results/interaction_evidence.md.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Policy recommendations, in priority order. (1) Add one ID-check officer during the burst window (modeled M1: peak mean wait 153.2 -> 48.6 min, std 75.0 -> 17.1 min, P(>90 min) -> 0). Because the burst is predictable (it tracks flight-schedule clustering at a fixed time each day), this can be a scheduled peak shift rather than permanent staffing: off-peak the checkpoint is already healthy (base 18-20 min, 0% over 45 min), so the marginal officer is used ~2-3 h/day. This is the highest-leverage, lowest-risk change. (2) Convert the two separate ID-officer queues to one shared single queue (modeled M4): zero capital cost, immediate, removes the variance penalty of the polling discipline; combine with (1) for the recommended configuration (M1+M4b). (3) Do NOT spend on body-scan or X-ray lanes (modeled M2, M3: zero peak effect) - keep them at 2 lanes as headroom; revisit only if a future data revision shows the body scan becoming the bottleneck. (4) Invest in pre-prepared-bins (M5) conditionally: it is style-conditional (Task 3), so pair it with a PreCheck-style pre-prep campaign for populations where bin prep is slow, and skip it where travelers already self-organize. (5) Use P(wait > 45 min) and std(wait) as the daily operating KPIs, not mean wait: the tail is what misses flights, and the model shows mean wait can look acceptable (153 min mean hides a 262-min p95) while the tail is catastrophic. (6) If a second burst hour appears in more data, raise K_ID to 4 (modeled: 16.8/5.1 min, 0% over 45 min) rather than adding body/x-ray capacity. Model status: VALIDATED - exact FCFS M/G/c event simulation (no formula approximation in the base model), 5/5 validation checks pass (unit tests vs hand computation; work conservation exact; M/M/c simulation within the Erlang-C band at ratio 0.65; strict monotonicity in staffing; data anchor reproduces the observed queue-depth order of magnitude and its monotone-growth mechanism). Strengths: both tracks coupled at exit; parameters fully provenanced (dataset or cited retrieval); honest negative results (M2/M3/M5/M6); style-robustness of the main recommendation; the model's central qualitative claim (congestion does not self-clear at observed staffing) is directly supported by the data's monotone queue growth. Weaknesses: S_ID from n = 7-9 logged officer shifts (likely including non-passenger work, the largest parameter risk - the model's peak numbers scale with it, so a sensitivity band on S_ID of [400, 900] s would be the first refinement); peak rate from a single burst; Poisson arrivals miss flight-schedule clustering (the burst is endogenous); secondaries are Bernoulli, not alarm-driven; 45-min horizon from operational practice (retrieved), not data. Future work: (a) multi-day data to fit the burst as a scheduled load profile and fit S_ID from per-passenger (not shift-level) logs; (b) model the endogenous burst (arrivals correlated with flight departure waves) and test whether peak-only dynamic staffing (modeled M6-style, applied to the ID stage) beats a fixed extra officer; (c) couple secondaries to scanner alarms and model the downstream knock-on when a body lane is held by a pat-down; (d) optimize the K_ID(t) schedule over the day under a labor-budget constraint, using P(wait > 45 min) as the service-level target.
